title: What's Next in Justice Tech: ITC and LSC's New Tech Report — full episode transcript
pub: Talk Justice, Legal Services Corporation / Legal Talk Network
author: Luigi Bai · Katie Strickfaden · Selena N. Hunn

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Justice capacity: AI potential requires deliberate implementation
st.an: The source accepts that technology can promote access to justice only through deliberate implementation and materially develops that proposition with concrete recommendations: more responsive funding, baseline technological capacity, flexible impact evaluation, documentation and cross-organisational learning. It treats these as implementation priorities rather than evidence that access outcomes have already improved.
qs: And that one’s related to developing a flexible evaluation framework to support our grantees, to support their innovation, their ability to measure impact, and document that so that we can use comprehensive evaluations and share those across the community so that grantees can use those to innovate and replicate.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts AI as supervised augmentation rather than wholesale substitution and materially extends the cluster with a legal-aid implementation roadmap centred on leadership, adoption, baseline capacity, change management, funding and impact evaluation. It is careful to present access-to-justice benefits and replication as intended outcomes rather than established sector-wide results, though it offers little direct evidence on verification or the jagged capability frontier.
qs: And that one’s related to developing a flexible evaluation framework to support our grantees, to support their innovation, their ability to measure impact, and document that so that we can use comprehensive evaluations and share those across the community so that grantees can use those to innovate and replicate.

st.t: Justice augmentation: Activity exceeds proven access gains
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s access-to-justice framing by treating technology as a means to expand legal help and by prioritising responsive funding and sector-wide participation. Its emphasis on grantmaking and collective responsibility supports the cluster’s institutional agenda, while its lack of effectiveness or outcome evidence reinforces the distinction between activity and proven access gains.

st.t: Legal-aid technology: Infrastructure matters beyond tool grants
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s broad framing by presenting technology and AI as tools to explore for improving legal-service delivery, not as proven standalone solutions, and by grounding the agenda in a broad, multi-sector consultation process. It does not independently substantiate implementation effectiveness, client protections or access outcomes.
qs: And given how much has evolved and how rapidly technology is evolving, particularly with AI, we thought it was most responsive for us to explore how to leverage these developments and improve the delivery of legal services and advance access to justice.

We had a lot of stakeholder involvement from folks outside of LSC across our grantee community, folks in academia, the courts, and technologists, and I’m sure I’m leaving out other groups, but just want to emphasize that it was a broad spectrum of participants who had input into the recommendations that this report produced.

kp.k: LSC's technology recommendations arose from multi-year stakeholder consultation
kp.d: Selena Hunn describes The Next Frontier: Harnessing Technology to Close the Justice Gap as an update to LSC's 2012, 2013 technology summit report, prompted particularly by rapid AI developments. Work launched in late 2023 and continued through 2024 into 2025, using interviews, focus groups, a 2024 ITC workshop convening more than 50 experts, and working groups. The resulting seven recommendations address LSC grantmaking and oversight as well as broader sector responsibilities; this is a consultative policy exercise, not a measured demonstration of AI's effects.
qs: we launched this project in late 2023, really throughout 2024 and into 2025 with the goal of updating our 2012, 2013 technology summit report.
we held a workshop at ITC in 2024. And the purpose of that was to convene more than 50 experts from various sectors.

the ultimate goal was to not only develop recommendations that would inform how LSC can be more responsive in its grant making and funding of legal aid or legal services technology projects and solutions, but also implore the broader sector to accept this charge

kp.k: Technology should become core legal aid work
kp.d: Katie Strickfaden supports the recommendation to treat technology as integral to legal aid's mission. Drawing on supportive leadership at Lakeshore Legal Aid, she argues that leadership backing makes technology projects easier and that explicit recognition can reduce reluctance to commit staff time and money. This is practitioner experience and a recommendation, rather than quantified evidence of organizational performance.
qs: One of the recommendations is about seeing technology as an important part of the core work that Legal Aids do.
I am very lucky at Lakeshore Legal Aid that my leader and the CEO of Lakeshore is very supportive of technology work
I think will help a lot of legal aid folks kind of shake off the fear of spending resources, time resources, fiscal resources on technology projects.

kp.k: AI adoption requires practical training across legal aid roles
kp.d: Strickfaden reports that Lakeshore's internal AI experimentation prompted staff requests for basic practical guidance. She believes most roles could be augmented by AI, rather than describing staff substitution. Lakeshore and other legal aid programs are compiling role-specific conversations into guidance and exercises for other organizations; the intended benefits remain prospective. Host Cat Moon identifies responsible AI innovation and broader technology adoption as the report's sixth recommendation.
qs: a lot of staff have come to us with questions like, “Everyone talks about AI, but I don’t know how to use it. Can you help me? ”
I think most roles could be augmented in some way by AI assistance.
give people some practical guide and exercises that they can hopefully take back with them to their legal aid.
six is lead and coordinate responsible AI innovation and broader tech adoption.

kp.k: AI drafting can support disabled legal professionals
kp.d: Strickfaden describes her own ADHD-related difficulty translating ideas into professional written communication. She reports that describing her ideas to AI provides a starting draft that she subsequently edits and may re-prompt, saving her time and distress. This is an individual account of assistive augmentation, not evidence establishing effects across disabilities or the profession; her planned session aims to help others explore similar support.
qs: I have ADHD and I will have this beautiful vision of an idea in my head and I will struggle with executive dysfunction and getting it down on paper in a way that is an appropriate professional communication to people who need to hear it.
obviously then take and tweak and change and maybe change the prompts
really, really saves me a lot of time and angst that I can’t get it out of my head and on paper.

kp.k: User feedback and change management condition technology adoption
kp.d: Strickfaden warns that attractive tools can fail to secure adoption if staff or client needs were not heard. She also reports that Lakeshore's 2022 case-management implementation exposed differing leadership attitudes toward change; a gamified exercise made those differences visible and shaped subsequent internal conversations and her work. These are implementation lessons from practice, without quantified adoption outcomes.
qs: no one’s going to adopt and use it because of something we didn’t hear about from impacted staff or client groups or whoever the tool is intended to serve.
it was 2022. We implemented a new case management system and that was a huge change for Lakeshore Legal Aid and the others in the state who adopted the same program.
It was an icebreaker exercise that was about like really answering questions and figuring out where you are on the change management comfort spectrum.

kp.k: Uneven readiness requires infrastructure support and flexible evaluation
kp.d: Hunn emphasizes variation in grantees' technology infrastructure and innovation readiness. She identifies recommendations to streamline resources for meeting and exceeding technology baselines and to modernize Technology Initiative Grant evaluation through a flexible framework for measuring and documenting impact, sharing evaluations, and enabling replication. Separately, Moon identifies data-driven decision-making as recommendation four; Strickfaden endorses its importance but describes using data as personally intimidating.
qs: we have grantees that are all across the spectrum as far as their technology infrastructure and their readiness for tech innovation.
streamline access to resources to help grantees meet and exceed the technology baselines.

developing a flexible evaluation framework to support our grantees, to support their innovation, their ability to measure impact, and document that so that we can use comprehensive evaluations and share those across the community so that grantees can use those to innovate and replicate.
four is promote and support data driven decision making.

kp.k: Sustainability funding supports replication beyond initial technology projects
kp.d: Luigi Bai endorses the report's third recommendation, exploring new technology funding approaches. He reports using sustainability, extension and adoption funding to take an initial TIG project through another funding round, add legal aid partners, and test replication. He considers this money well invested, but does not report a measured return or establish ecosystem-wide replicability.
qs: number three, explore new funding approaches for technology projects.
we definitely appreciate and have taken advantage of the new SEA funding, which is sustainability, extension and adoption.

That’s helped us take an initial TIG project and do a second round of funding to bring this to other partners, other legal aids, and test out how this can be replicable across the whole legal aid ecosystem.

kp.k: Self-help technology aims to extend access with professional guidance
kp.d: Bai argues that people can address their own legal problems with good guidance, particularly from licensed professionals. He supports modernizing high-quality self-help tools through collaboration and integration. As an illustration of possible efficiency, he references a Maryland group's planned presentation about software helping it reach, in his qualified recollection, about 18,000 people a year; the transcript does not independently evaluate that result. Moon separately stresses intentional, thoughtful and careful implementation.
qs: I’m a firm believer that people can help themselves with their legal problems as long as they get some good guidance from especially licensed professionals.
That’s the group out of Maryland who’s going to talk about some software that they’ve put together to help them reach, I think, about 18,000 people a year.
There are sub recommendations in there about more collaboration, encouraging more integration.
we need to be very intentional, thoughtful, and careful about how that happens.

kp.k: LACI targets legal information maintenance rather than wholesale review
kp.d: Bai describes Legal Aid Content Intelligence (LACI) as software that checks online legal authorities weekly or monthly, depending on configuration, and alerts staff to documents needing review. He contrasts this with periodic review of entire document collections, which can waste effort on unchanged material while leaving intervening changes unaddressed. The described mechanism prioritizes human review; it is not presented as AI autonomously updating legal advice, and no quantified savings are supplied.
qs: Lacey is spelled L-A-C-I, and it stands for Legal Aid Content Intelligence
sometimes when you do all of this work to review, a lot of the stuff hasn’t changed, but you’ve spent that work anyway.

What Lacey does is it’s constantly on a weekly or monthly basis, depending on how you configure it, checking to see if any of these things change and alerting you to which documents need to be reviewed.
So you’re not reviewing all the documents all the time, but you also aren’t letting things get stale for too long.

kp.k: Open-source licensing enables shared legal aid infrastructure
kp.d: Bai reports that Lone Star developed LACI over two TIGs and released it under the AGPL free software license to permit use, adaptation and contributed changes. Texas Legal Services Center and Idaho Legal Aid Services are adapting it in different environments; Atlanta Legal Aid received a TIG award for Georgia adaptation. Bai recommends considering open-source licenses for shareable grant outputs and community building. LACI adaptation depends on relevant authorities being available online.
qs: we’ve released this to the public under a free software license called the AGPL.
This is a license that allows anyone to pick up the software, use it right away, adapt it for their state, to also propose adding changes to the code so that other people can use it.
we’ve included two partners, Texas Legal Services Center and Idaho Legal Aid Services who are adapting LACI in their own environments in two different ways.
if you’re in a state where your stuff is online, you too can adapt Lacey.

kp.k: Proposed AI assistance would identify authorities for content monitoring
kp.d: Bai identifies a labor-intensive prerequisite for LACI: documents lacking citations require retrospective legal research to identify relevant authorities. He describes Atlanta Legal Aid's planned exploration of machine learning and possibly generative AI, and suggests that data from participating organizations might train a model to propose authorities for monitoring. This is a prospective capability expressed tentatively, not a deployed or validated AI result.
qs: Atlanta Legal Aid who just got a TIG award to adapt Lacey in their state in Georgia and also look into ways of using machine learning and maybe some generative AI techniques
if you don’t have citations in your documents that say what are the relevant authorities, you have to go back kind of forensically and do that legal research

we may be able to use the data that we’ve collected at Lone Star and maybe with TLSC and iLIS to train up a model that maybe can help other organizations then put their documents in and say, “Here are a suggested set of authorities for you to monitor.”

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Speakers describe AI as a means of augmenting legal-aid staff, supporting disabled professionals, modernizing intake, and potentially identifying legal authorities for content maintenance.
pts.d: Katie Strickfaden believes AI could augment most roles in a legal-aid organization. She describes her own use of AI to turn ideas into draft professional communications, helping with ADHD-related executive dysfunction and saving time and frustration. Luigi Bai describes a prospective extension to Legal Aid Content Intelligence (LACI): machine learning, and possibly generative AI, could suggest authorities relevant to an organization's documents so those authorities can be monitored. This is a proposed capability, not a demonstrated feature of LACI; its existing monitoring and alerting functions are not identified as AI. Selena Hunn reports that an upcoming conference session will demonstrate intake transformations using accessible client-centered technologies and AI, without specifying AI's separate contribution or measured results. Bai also observes increasing attempts to deploy predictive AI or machine learning to assist people or allocate resources, but does not state a specific beneficial or harmful outcome from those deployments.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is practitioner experience, internal conversations, project plans, and descriptions of forthcoming demonstrations—not quantified AI performance or impact findings.
pts.d: Strickfaden grounds her accessibility claim in personal experience and her broader augmentation expectation in conversations with Lakeshore staff and other legal-aid programs. Bai points to Atlanta Legal Aid's TIG award and existing organizational data as a basis for exploring an authority-suggestion model, but reports no trained-model results. Hunn previews grantee intake demonstrations rather than presenting their findings. The broader technology report draws on stakeholder interviews, focus groups, a 2024 workshop involving more than 50 experts, and working groups; this establishes its consultative basis, not empirical validation of particular AI benefits. The transcript supplies no AI benchmarks, quantified time savings, accuracy measures, or causal evidence that AI closes the justice gap. The approximately 18,000 people served annually mentioned elsewhere concerns brief-advice software, not an explicitly AI-based intervention.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current individual AI use is distinguished from exploratory projects and upcoming demonstrations; benefits depend on human adaptation, implementation capacity, and suitable data.
pts.d: At the time of this 2026 episode, Strickfaden describes current AI-assisted drafting and ongoing safe experimentation at Lakeshore. Her account is augmentation: she edits drafts and changes prompts rather than relying on autonomous output. Bai's suggested-authorities model remains explicitly tentative, with no completion date, and would potentially use data from Lone Star and partner organizations. LACI's existing operation requires online authorities; documents lacking relevant citations require retrospective legal research, the burden the proposed model might help address. Hunn's intake examples and AI-capacity session are scheduled for the upcoming January 2026 conference, not presented as completed evaluations in the episode. Hunn also notes uneven technology infrastructure and readiness among grantees. Strickfaden's broader technology-adoption discussion emphasizes staff and client feedback and buy-in, but does not establish an AI-specific adoption result. The report-development process ran from late 2023 through 2025; that period is not an AI-impact measurement window.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The focus is nonprofit legal-aid staff and organizations, disabled legal professionals, and the clients and communities they serve.
pts.d: Strickfaden anticipates support across numerous legal-aid roles, not just attorneys, and highlights professionals whose disabilities create barriers to drafting or communicating ideas. Bai's proposed authority-suggestion capability targets organizations maintaining legal-information documents, including self-help websites, client template memos, and outreach handouts; more efficient maintenance could support the people relying on that information, although no AI-specific client outcome is demonstrated. Hunn frames AI capacity building and intake modernization around resource-constrained legal-aid providers meeting client needs. Bai identifies clients and communities as affected by predictive systems used for assistance or resource allocation, without detailing the direction or scale of those effects. The episode does not predict law-firm staffing reductions, lawyer replacement, billing changes, or legal-market revenue shifts.
